description: We are a curious team that is interested in coding and space. By combining our skills in software, data research, and design, we aim to help map the path for humanity on Mars.
summary:
When astronauts walk on Mars they are essentially on their own. And because of the communication delay they would not have enough time to get advice from Earth when things get tough. So we built Mars Maps to solve this. It is a mission-critical tool that helps astronauts plan their paths and stay safe on their journey. 

Using real NASA data such as terrain maps from the exact path Curiosity rover drove, live weather feeds, and radiation models to help astronauts plan their routes, check oxygen limits, and spot hazards in 3D before stepping outside. If an emergency happens, like an oxygen leak or a solar storm, Mars Maps instantly compares the risk and calculates the safest way back to base. We did not rely on abstract simulations; we validated our math against the actual paths of NASA's rovers to make sure our routes are scientifically sound. Mars Maps is not just a map it is a reliable safety net for human exploration.
details:
How it works:
MarsMaps has two sides: a planning console for the crew to use at their base, and a "Helmet HUD" for the walk itself. It’s like a smart GPS for Mars, but one that worries about oxygen and safety. It uses an algorithm to find the safest path, constantly checking slope hazards and sand traps. We built the "intelligence" based on human physics: it calculates how much oxygen a human in a suit actually burns on a slope (using NASA’s metabolic models). In an emergency, it pauses the mission and tells the crew: "Turn back now, or you'll run out of air."

Benefits & Impact:
The biggest problem on Mars is the "Latency Paradox"—you need help now, but it's 20 minutes away. MarsMaps gives astronauts the independence to make safe, split-second decisions. By automating the safety checks, we reduce the stress on the crew, letting them focus on what they came there to do: the science.

Tools & Technologies:
We wanted the app to be fast and reliable, so we skipped complex AI in favor of robust, deterministic physics and geometry:

  • Data: We used NASA's Mars Trek APIs (HiRISE/CTX terrain), Curiosity’s own weather logs (REMS/RAD), and space weather forecasts.
  • The Tech: It’s built with TypeScript, Leaflet for maps, and Three.js for the 3D helmet view. We used Python to process the terrain data beforehand.
  • Offline First: The app runs locally in the browser. It doesn't need an internet connection to work—critical for a planet with no Wi-Fi.

Creativity & Factors Considered:
Our "secret sauce" is Ground Truth. Instead of guessing if a path is walkable, we tested our math against the 38km track record of NASA's rovers. We checked our elevation data against 142 points where Curiosity actually parked, finding we were accurate within 40 centimeters. We didn’t just build a map; we built a system that respects the real, harsh physics of Mars. We designed this not for a computer to understand, but for an astronaut in a high-stress, high-stakes situation to use at a glance.
